subject: History
board: National Curriculum KS3 (History is not offered at KS4)
source: National Curriculum KS3 (challenges for Britain, Europe and the wider world, 1901 to the present day: the First World War); no school Drive history material for this unit, written from scratch

lessons.title: Why did war break out in 1914?
objectives: Explain the long-term causes of the First World War using MAIN
Describe how the assassination of Franz Ferdinand led to war

keywords.def: building up armed forces and believing in using them
an agreement between countries to support each other
building an empire by controlling other lands
strong pride in your nation, or wanting independence for it
the murder of an important person for political reasons

starter: Name two ways railways changed Britain.

teach.heading: Bismillah: a war that shook the world
bullets: The war lasted from 1914 to 1918
Millions of soldiers and civilians died
It began in Europe but became global
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and remind pupils that we study war to learn and to honour the value of peace and every human life. Ask what they know about the war from family or the media.

teach.heading: Long-term causes: MAIN
bullets: Militarism: arms races, especially naval
Alliances: Triple Alliance and Triple Entente
Imperialism and Nationalism created rivalry
teach.note: Use MAIN as a memory device. Germany and Britain raced to build battleships (Dreadnoughts). Imperial rivalry over colonies in Africa. Nationalism in the Balkans. Ask pupils which cause seems the most dangerous.

teach.heading: The Balkans
bullets: Austria-Hungary controlled Bosnia
Serbia wanted Slavic people to be independent
The region was called the 'powder keg'
teach.note: Explain that Bosnia was annexed by Austria-Hungary in 1908. Many Serbs wanted Bosnia to join Serbia. Locate the Balkans on a map.

teach.heading: 28 June 1914
bullets: Archduke Franz Ferdinand visited Sarajevo
Gavrilo Princip shot him and his wife Sophie
Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia
teach.note: The assassination was the 'spark', not the whole cause. Follow the chain: Austria declares war on Serbia (28 July); Russia mobilises; Germany declares war on Russia and France; Germany invades Belgium; Britain declares war on 4 August 1914.

practice: Which two alliances existed in Europe in 1914?
Why was the assassination the spark but not the only cause?
independent: Draw a flow diagram from the assassination to Britain joining the war
Write an explanation of one long-term cause and one short-term cause
Rank the four MAIN causes from most to least important and justify your top choice
exit: Which German action brought Britain into the war?
lessons.homework: Write six sentences explaining why the First World War began, using at least three keywords.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: flow diagram with missing words supplied. Stretch: explain why historians disagree about which cause was most important.

lessons.title: Life in the trenches on the Western Front
objectives: Describe the stalemate on the Western Front
Explain what daily life in the trenches was like

keywords.def: the line of fighting in France and Belgium
a situation where neither side can win
the area between opposing trenches
a long deep ditch dug for soldiers to shelter in
a mental illness caused by the stress of war

starter: Which country did Britain defend by declaring war?
Which event started the war on 28 June 1914?

teach.heading: The Schlieffen Plan fails
bullets: Germany planned to defeat France quickly
Belgium resisted and Britain sent an army
The Allies stopped Germany at the Marne in 1914
teach.note: Explain that the plan was to knock out France in about six weeks before turning on Russia. After the Marne, both sides dug in. Use a map.

teach.heading: Trench warfare
bullets: Trenches stretched from the sea to Switzerland
Machine guns and barbed wire protected them
Attacks over no man's land cost many lives
teach.note: Show a diagram of the trench system: front line, support, reserve. Ask why defence was stronger than attack at this time.

teach.heading: Daily life
bullets: Soldiers faced mud, rats and lice
Trench foot caused painful, sometimes fatal, infection
Food was basic: bully beef and biscuits
teach.note: Use extracts from letters and photos. Remind pupils to weigh evidence: soldiers' letters were censored. Include humour and comradeship as well as horror.

teach.heading: Mental and spiritual strain
bullets: Constant shelling caused shell shock
Soldiers turned to prayer and friendship
Many were never the same again
teach.note: Be sensitive: some pupils may have family connections to war. Mention that religion mattered to many soldiers, including Muslim soldiers who prayed in the field when they could.

practice: Name two dangers soldiers faced in the trenches.
independent: Draw and label a cross-section of the trench system
Write a letter home from a soldier describing one day in the trenches
Explain in a paragraph why the war on the Western Front became a stalemate
exit: Give one reason the Western Front was a stalemate.
lessons.homework: Find one image or source from the trenches and write what it tells us about soldiers' lives.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: letter frame with sentence starters. Stretch: assess how useful a soldier's letter is as evidence of trench life.

lessons.title: The Battle of the Somme, 1916
objectives: Evaluate whether the Somme was a failure

keywords.def: the river valley in France where a huge battle began in July 1916
soldiers killed, wounded, captured or missing
artillery fire that moves forward just ahead of advancing soldiers
a unit of men from the same town who joined up together
Sir Douglas Haig, the British commander on the Western Front

starter: Name two hardships of trench life.

teach.heading: Why attack on the Somme?
bullets: The Allies wanted to break the stalemate
They hoped to relieve pressure on the French at Verdun
Britain had a new army of volunteers
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Explain that Verdun, a German attack on the French from February 1916, was draining the French army. Many British soldiers in 1916 were volunteers from Kitchener's army.

teach.heading: The plan
bullets: A week of shelling was meant to destroy German defences
Soldiers would walk across no man's land
The infantry attack began on 1 July at 7.30 am
teach.note: Many shells were duds and German dugouts survived. Ask: why did the Allies expect the attack to be easy? Important: do not blame all commanders with simplistic claims; discuss different views.

teach.heading: 1 July 1916
bullets: About 57,000 British casualties in one day
Nearly 19,000 men were killed
It remains the worst day in British army history
teach.note: These figures are widely cited: 57,470 casualties, 19,240 killed. Give them as 'about'. Mention the Pals battalions, where whole communities lost sons together.

teach.heading: The battle continues
bullets: The fighting went on until November 1916
Allies advanced about 6 miles
Total casualties on all sides were over a million
teach.note: Ask: was it worth it? Discuss different interpretations: some historians say it wore down Germany and taught lessons; others see needless slaughter. Tanks were first used on the Somme in September 1916.

practice: Why did the Allies attack on the Somme?
How many British soldiers were casualties on the first day (about)?
independent: Write a news report on the first day of the Somme
Create a 'for and against' table: was the Somme a failure?
Write a paragraph giving your judgement on whether the Somme was a failure, using evidence
exit: On what date did the Battle of the Somme begin?
Give one reason historians disagree about the Somme.
lessons.homework: Research a Pals battalion and write three facts about it.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: report template with a word bank. Stretch: evaluate two historians' interpretations of Haig.

lessons.title: A world war: soldiers from the Empire and Muslim soldiers
objectives: Explain how people from the British Empire contributed to the war
Describe the experiences of Muslim soldiers in the First World War

keywords.def: countries and territories controlled by Britain
the British-run army in India, with many Muslim and Sikh soldiers
something given to help achieve a result
something built to remember people who died
remembering an event or people with a special act

starter: When did the Battle of the Somme begin?
Name one country in the British Empire in 1914.

teach.heading: A global war
bullets: Britain's Empire supplied soldiers and workers
Troops came from India, Africa, the Caribbean and elsewhere
Fighting spread to the Middle East and Africa
teach.note: Start with bismillah. Show a map of the Empire. Ask pupils which of these places they or their families link to. Emphasise this is history for all of us.

teach.heading: The Indian Army
bullets: Over a million Indian soldiers served overseas
Many were Muslims, Sikhs and Hindus
They fought in France, Mesopotamia and elsewhere
teach.note: The Indian Army had large numbers of Muslim soldiers. Indian troops arrived in France in late 1914 and fought at Neuve Chapelle in 1915. Say 'over a million' as it is a standard summary figure.

teach.heading: Faith in the field
bullets: Muslim soldiers prayed and fasted where they could
The Shah Jahan Mosque in Woking served Muslim soldiers
Muslim burial grounds were set up near Woking
teach.note: Woking's Shah Jahan Mosque (1889) was used for prayer by Indian Muslim soldiers, and a burial ground was created at Horsell Common for those who died in British hospitals. Ask why respecting faith helped morale.

teach.heading: Remembering
bullets: The Menin Gate in Belgium lists missing soldiers
India Gate in Delhi remembers Indian soldiers
Many contributions were forgotten for years
teach.note: Discuss why some groups' stories were left out of history and why they matter now. Link to the role of remembering with gratitude. Remembrance Sunday falls in November; discuss respectful ways to remember.

practice: Name two groups who came from the Empire to fight.
Why was the Woking mosque important?
independent: Produce a fact file: Muslim soldiers in the First World War
Write a speech for Remembrance Day mentioning soldiers from the Empire
Answer in a paragraph: Why is it important to include all soldiers in the story of the First World War?
exit: Name one country that sent soldiers to fight for Britain.
Why should we remember the contribution of all soldiers?
lessons.homework: Interview a family member about a story of remembrance, or research one soldier from the Empire.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: fact file with images and word bank. Stretch: evaluate how well history textbooks represent soldiers from the Empire.
